title: Three Crowns and a Divided Realm

title_i18n.en: Three Crowns and a Divided Realm

subtitle: Santivarma and the Birth of the Triparvatha Line
era: Santivarma and the Triparvatha split, c. 450-475 CE
region: Talagunda, Banavasi and the debated Triparvatha country
moral: Shared power can protect a realm and endanger it at once.

sources.citation: Talagunda pillar inscription, v. 34; Kielhorn, Epigraphia Indica 8 (1906)
sources.note: Names Santivarma, three crowns and poet Kubja's commissioned inscription.

sources.citation: Halasi copper plates of Mrigeshavarma; G.S. Gai, Inscriptions of the Early Kadambas (1996)
sources.note: Evidence for succession after Santivarma and later conflict.

sources.citation: George M. Moraes, The Kadamba Kula (1931), pp. 28-30; Noboru Karashima ed., A Concise History of South India (2014), p. 369
sources.note: Historical reconstruction of the split and chronology.

panels.shot: sweeping low-angle wide of a king framed by three distant hill-forts

dialogue.text: In the stone of Talagunda he is praised as wearing three crowns, yet Santivarma’s greatest act split his own house and birthed the shadowy realm of Triparvatha.

panels.shot: slow push-in on inscription being carved with king watching

dialogue.text: Around 450 CE, in the Brahmana village of Talagunda, a Kadamba king ordered his story cut into stone, calling on the poet Kubja to bind his name to eternity.

panels.shot: medium shot over Santivarma’s shoulder toward the sculptor and half-finished pillar

dialogue.text: This Talagunda pillar, later read by scholars like Kielhorn, would remember Santivarma as the son of Kakusthavarma, a king adorned, it says, with three shining crowns.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on Santivarma’s face, eyes reflecting three vague crowns

dialogue.text: Were these crowns just words for glory, or the memory of real diadems, of real thrones in Banavasi and beyond that Kakusthavarma had once bent to Kadamba power?

panels.shot: bird’s-eye wide of Banavasi city and palace complex amid forests and river

dialogue.text: Banavasi was the heart of Kadamba power, a forest kingdom turned royal city, grown strong under Mayurasharma and Kakusthavarma between the pull of Pallava and the shadow of the Vakatakas.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of throne room with counselors and maps laid on a low table

dialogue.text: Santivarma inherited a realm woven by alliances, Kadamba charters at Halasi and beyond showing lineages and grants, even as Pallava power pressed from the east and frontier hills stirred in the west.

panels.shot: slow push-in on map segment showing Banavasi and a rough ‘Triparvatha’ hill cluster

dialogue.text: Later scholars like Moraes and Karashima would search these hills for Triparvatha, debating whether it lay near present-day Dharwad, another node in the chain of Deccan strongholds.

panels.shot: medium shot of Santivarma in discussion with a younger warrior-prince-like figure (shown only in silhouette, unnamed)

dialogue.text: The inscriptions do not narrate his councils, yet the later rise of a Krishnavarma at Triparvatha hints at a younger cadet branch coming into its own under the weight of growing threats.

panels.shot: low-angle medium shot of Santivarma placing a small crown beside his own on a ritual tray

dialogue.text: Some modern historians see in his three crowns a sign that one Kadamba realm was being shared, the main line at Banavasi and a cadet at Triparvatha, dividing authority between centre and frontier.

panels.shot: wide shot of a rugged hill-fort landscape with a garrison drilling, Santivarma in the foreground

dialogue.text: To guard these hills from Pallava raids and rival chiefs, a second seat of power at Triparvatha may have seemed wise, a shield turned outward even as it created another centre of loyalty.

panels.shot: close-up on Santivarma’s hand resting on the rough stone of a hill bastion, distant plains visible

dialogue.speaker: santivarma
dialogue.text: A house that holds the hills holds its fate. But will it hold together?

panels.shot: medium interior shot of priests and scribes preparing copper plates, Santivarma overseeing

dialogue.text: Copper plates from Halasi, later studied by G.S. Gai, trace how power flowed after Santivarma, naming successors in Banavasi even as another line at Triparvatha began to leave its own imprints.

panels.shot: wide shot of a ceremonial assembly with two thrones set slightly apart

dialogue.text: The record is silent on a formal division, yet the later coexistence of Banavasi and Triparvatha branches suggests that under Santivarma the seeds of a shared sovereignty were sown.

panels.shot: medium shot with soft focus, Santivarma slightly older, looking at the Talagunda pillar now fully raised

dialogue.text: Verse by verse, the Talagunda inscription weaves his lineage, tracing Mayurasharma’s rise and Kakusthavarma’s alliances, then resting on Santivarma, the king who shines, it claims, with the splendour of three crowns.

panels.shot: extreme close-up on a specific line of the inscription, letters crisp and deep

dialogue.text: Later readers in distant libraries would pause at this phrase, puzzling over what these ‘three crowns’ meant in practice, and how they foreshadowed the branching of the Kadamba house.

panels.shot: montage-like wide shot half-shadowed: one side Banavasi palace, other side a hill-fort labeled by architecture as different seat

dialogue.text: After his time, the Banavasi line and the Triparvatha line stood side by side, sometimes cooperating, sometimes colliding, their grants and titles revealing a realm both defended and divided.

panels.shot: medium shot in a darkened council hall, two groups of nobles facing each other warily, empty throne between

dialogue.text: The Halasi plates of Mrigeshavarma hint at later conflicts, the calm legal formulas of donations masking struggles over precedence and control between branches that shared a name but not always a will.

panels.shot: slow pull-back from Santivarma’s statue-like image fading into bare pillar and scattered ruins

dialogue.text: Santivarma’s own end slips through the gaps of time; what endures is stone and copper, from which historians must reconstruct how a king holding three crowns left behind a house with more than one throne.

panels.shot: high wide shot of modern scholars at a table with photos of inscriptions, Santivarma’s ghostly outline above

dialogue.text: His story reminds us that sharing power can be a fortress and a fault-line, and that even in our time, every divided realm carries the echo of Santivarma’s three unseen crowns.
